parole.significato: A flag or standard used by a military commander, monarch or nation.
parole.testo: From Middle English baner, from Old French baniere (Modern bannière), of Germanic origin. More at band.

parole.significato: To secure or steady; cause to come to a fixed position or state; bring to a halt or stop.
parole.testo: From be- + stay, from Middle English *stayen, steyen, from Old French estaier, estayer (“to prop, stay, support”), from estaye (“prop, support”), of Proto-Germanic origin. More at stay.

parole.significato: A serious criminal offense, which, under United States federal law, is punishable by a term of imprisonment of not less…
parole.testo: From Middle English felony, felonie, from Old French felonie (“evil, immoral deed”), from felon (“evildoer”). Ultimately of Proto-Germanic origin. More at felon. By surface analysis, felon + -y.

parole.significato: A sharp instrument used to open a vein, to lance gums, or the like.
parole.testo: From Middle English fleme, fleom, from Old French flieme, flemie (“open vein”), probably via a Proto-Germanic source (compare Old Saxon flēma, Old High German fliotuma, fliodema, Old English flȳtme (“fleam, lancet”)), borrowed from Vulgar Latin fletoma, *fletomus, from Late Latin flebotomus, phlebot

parole.significato: Of hair, to form into a mass of tight curls.
parole.testo: From Middle English frysen, from Old French friser, frizer (“to frizzle, crisp, curl, ruffle, braid, touch lightly, graze, scratch”), of Proto-Germanic origin, perhaps via Old Frankish *fris (“curl”), from Proto-Germanic *frisaz (“frizzy, curly”). parole.significato: No longer fresh, in reference to food, urine, straw, wounds, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English stale, from Old French estal (“fixed position, place”), but probably originally from Proto-Germanic *stāną (“to stand”): compare West Flemish stel in the same sense for ‘beer’ and ‘urine’.
